A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CARL and CARL-SSL with the same research objectives and principal experiments. Text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison across the revised layout.

before.justification: v1 reports original medical camera-simulation experiments, urban scene segmentation, satellite land-cover segmentation, and architectural ablations in Sections 4–5.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds HyperFree comparisons, including medical robustness and HSICity segmentation results.

M1.justification: The wavelength Fourier encoding, alternating spectral self-attention and query cross-attention, query summation, spatial encoder, and joint spectral/spatial VICReg training remain unchanged. The new appendix pseudocode documents these existing procedures.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same porcine organ data and simulated cameras, Cityscapes/HSICity segmentation, HyKo-VIS and HSIDrive pre-training data, and HySpecNet-11k-to-SegMunich transfer. The added comparisons introduce no distinct task, domain, or camera test scenario.

E2.justification: v2 adds HyperFree adaptations to the medical and automotive comparisons and the computational comparison in Appendix B. Table 2 also adds ViT and ViT-22k baselines. This substantially broadens the evaluated comparator set, particularly by including another wavelength-aware, channel-adaptive approach.

E3.justification: The added comparisons introduce HyperFree configurations using ViT for medical evaluation, SwinMask2Former for automotive evaluation, and EVA-02 for FLOP measurement. Table 2 adds ViT comparisons without pre-training and with ImageNet-22k initialization. Existing splits, simulation settings, metrics, and CARL configurations remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 5 extends the existing progressive spectral-heterogeneity robustness test with a HyperFree curve, and Appendix B extends the computational-cost analysis to HyperFree. The wavelength-encoding and query-count ablations in Table 3 are unchanged; the qualitative examples are retained in merged figures.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% confidence intervals for the same types of results. HyperFree receives the existing uncertainty-reporting treatment, but v2 adds no repeated-run counts, seeds, significance tests, or explanation of confidence-interval estimation.

E6.justification: New results span all three domains: HyperFree's medical robustness curve and HSICity mIoU of 40.1, and SegMunich mIoUs of 44.1 for ViT and 45.2 for ViT-22k. The medical text replaces a 50.2-point advantage over Hyve with a 31.5-point advantage over HyperFree, reflecting a different comparator. Table 5 also changes Spectral Adapter's bicycle IoU from 20.0 to 11.3. Retained CARL headline scores are unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds explicit token-level mathematical definitions of the VICReg objective, including batchwise variance and covariance calculations in Equations 2–7; v1 described the components and weights without these definitions. No theorem or proof is added. The wavelength encoding and synthetic-filter mathematics remain equivalent.

C1.justification: The abstract and three introductory contributions retain their meaning. Section 6 adds an explicit priority claim for designing for and thoroughly evaluating spectral heterogeneity, modestly extending the earlier novelty claims about the architecture and self-supervised framework.

C2.justification: The expanded discussion attributes advantages over HyperFree to continuous wavelength encoding versus nearest-neighbor wavelength tokenization, especially for RGB integration. It also newly acknowledges cross-camera differences in imaging principles and illumination as limitations beyond spectral heterogeneity.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds forward-pass and SSL training pseudocode, explicit loss calculations, an EMA momentum schedule from 0.996 to 1.0, a minimum learning rate of 10^-5, and SSL batch size 16 on a 24GB GPU. The simulation description identifies the Ximea camera model. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to previously used settings.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around HyperFree and multimodal fusion approaches, discussing wavelength discretization, scalability, and assumptions about modality availability. It also acknowledges related wavelength encoding by Gonzalez Avilés et al. These additions go beyond reference renumbering or bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: Related work, the SSL explanation, experimental narratives, and ablation prose receive substantial rewriting and compression. The conclusion becomes an expanded Discussion, appendix explanations grow, and the acknowledgments disappear. The overall scientific section sequence remains recognizable.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. v2 redesigns and combines v1 Figures 1–2 into its Figure 1, redraws the architecture schematic, and merges v1 Figures 6–7 into Figure 4. Tables gain comparator rows or columns, and two algorithm displays are added.

improvement.justification: The HyperFree comparisons strengthen coverage of relevant alternatives, while the pseudocode and additional training details improve reproducibility. The new limitation discussion also improves qualification of applicability. These are useful refinements to an already established experimental account; the main results remain unchanged, and the stronger explanation favoring continuous wavelength encoding lacks a dedicated validating analysis.
